Maladaptive Strategies.value: Going to or near the place where the event happened
ruminate about how event could have been prevented

Threat.value: I feel on guard even inside my own home
I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly

Memory.value: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: For a childhood trauma defined as witnessing domestic violence, 'Body Shame' is hard to reconcile with the trauma type because it implies a direct bodily violation or injury to the patient rather than witnessing violence between others. While witness trauma can lead to guilt, fear, mistrust, or betrayal appraisals, shame specifically about 'what happened to my body' is clinically implausible here unless there is an additional unreported direct trauma.

issues.item: Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
issues.explanation: The memory profile centers on disorganized, overwhelmed recall of a witnessed domestic violence event. 'Auditory Recall' can occur in witness trauma, but in this profile it is the only strongly sensory-perceptual memory item and is not linked to any trigger items or matching contextual content. Given the formulation shows Triggers disconnected from Memory and the rest of the profile emphasizes global threat and appraisal-driven coping, this item stands out as poorly integrated and may reflect a different trauma presentation.

vignette:
Mariana, a 26-year-old school counselor of Latin American descent, still remembers the exact sound of a glass ashtray hitting the living room wall. She was seven years old, hiding behind the sofa in the small apartment she shared with her mother and her mother's boyfriend, Manuel. She had been told to stay in her room, but she had crept out to see why her mother was crying. What she saw was Manuel, drunk, shoving her mother against the kitchen counter while shouting that she had "made him do this." Mariana had tried to intervene, running into the room and pulling at Manuel's sleeve, begging him to stop. He had turned and backhanded her across the face, sending her sprawling. Her mother had screamed, and then the police had come-called by a neighbor-but by the time they arrived, Manuel was sitting calmly on the couch, and her mother, terrified and bruised, told the officers it was nothing, that she had fallen. The officers left. Nothing changed. Manuel stayed. And Mariana learned, at seven years old, that the people who were supposed to protect her-her mother, the police-would not. She came to believe, with a certainty that never faded, that the event had happened because of how she acted, because she had left her room, because she had tried to help. She had made it worse.

Now, nearly two decades later, Mariana works in a middle school in a suburban district, guiding children through their own confusions and hurts. She is good at her job, patient and kind, but she carries a constant, exhausting vigilance. She scans every room she enters for exits, for angles, for who might be angry. She cannot tolerate having her back to a door. In her own small apartment, she feels no safety; she sleeps with the lights on in the hallway and has installed a chain lock she checks three times before bed. The sound of a key in the lock, even her own, makes her heart stop. At work, she has learned to sit with her desk facing the door, her chair pushed against the wall so no one can approach from behind. When a student taps her shoulder unexpectedly, she flinches so hard that the child sometimes steps back, startled, and Mariana has to force a smile and apologize.

The memory of that night does not come to her as a coherent story she can tell. When a colleague asked, during a team-building exercise, about her "most challenging childhood experience," Mariana opened her mouth to describe the ashtray, the shouting, the taste of blood from her lip-and found herself unable to speak. The words scattered. She felt the same overwhelming heat and helplessness she had felt as a child, and she had to excuse herself to the bathroom, where she sat on the floor for ten minutes, shaking. The memory returns without warning: a certain smell of cooking oil, a man's raised voice in the hallway at school, even the particular quality of afternoon light slanting through blinds. Each time, it is as if she is back behind that sofa, small and frozen.

She has developed a quiet, methodical set of strategies to manage this. She avoids the street where her childhood apartment stood, taking a longer route home even if it adds twenty minutes to her commute. She replays the night in her mind, over and over, trying to find the exact moment where she could have acted differently-if she had stayed in her room, if she had not pulled on Manuel's sleeve, if she had screamed louder for the police to stay. These rumination sessions can last hours, leaving her drained and no closer to an answer. She has come to believe, deeply, that people cannot be trusted. She keeps her colleagues at a careful distance. She has not dated in three years; the thought of being vulnerable with a man, of letting him into her home, feels impossible.

What finally brought Mariana to seek help was a moment at work last month. A father, angry about a disciplinary action against his son, raised his voice in her office. It was not loud, not threatening-but the tone, the cadence, the way he pointed his finger, sent her into a full dissociative flashback. She could not respond. She sat frozen, staring, until the school principal intervened. The next day, her supervisor gently suggested she take some leave. Mariana is terrified of losing her job, the one place where she feels she has some purpose. She is hoping, though she cannot quite say it out loud, for a way to stop feeling like a seven-year-old girl hiding behind a sofa every time the world gets a little too loud.
